source.name: Congress.gov API, Library of Congress (current members)

descriptions.borough_ak: In Alaska, a borough is the local government that does many of the jobs a county does in other states, like schools, property taxes, and land-use planning.
descriptions.cdp: {name} is a census designated place: a community the Census Bureau names so it can count the people who live there. It has no city government of its own. Local services usually come from the county or township.
descriptions.census_area: Much of Alaska has no borough government. The Census Bureau splits that area into census areas so it can count the people who live there. A census area has no local government of its own.
descriptions.county: A county is a local government for part of a state. Depending on state law, counties often run local courts, property records, the sheriff's office, elections, and some roads.
descriptions.county_dc: The District of Columbia has no counties. Its own local government, a mayor and a council, runs both city and county services.
descriptions.district: A congressional district is the area that elects one member of the U.S. House of Representatives. Voters here choose that member every two years to vote on federal laws for them.
descriptions.district_at_large: {state} has only one seat in the U.S. House, so the whole state is one at-large district. Voters across {state} choose that member every two years to vote on federal laws for them.
descriptions.district_dc: The District of Columbia elects one Delegate to the U.S. House every two years. The Delegate can introduce bills, speak, and serve on committees, but cannot vote on passing laws.
descriptions.district_pr: Puerto Rico elects one Resident Commissioner to the U.S. House every four years. The Resident Commissioner can introduce bills, speak, and serve on committees, but cannot vote on passing laws.
descriptions.district_territory: {state} elects one Delegate to the U.S. House every two years. The Delegate can introduce bills, speak, and serve on committees, but cannot vote on passing laws.
descriptions.house_vacant: This seat is empty right now. A House seat is filled only by a special election.
descriptions.incorporated_place: {name} is an incorporated {kind} with its own local government, such as a mayor or a council. It often handles local police, zoning, parks, water, and streets, depending on state law.
descriptions.independent_city: {name} is an independent city. It is not part of any county, so the city government also does the jobs a county would, like local courts and property records.
descriptions.municipio: Puerto Rico is divided into municipalities (municipios). Each one has an elected mayor and a municipal legislature that run local services.
descriptions.officials_cdp: This community has no city officials of its own. County officials are not listed yet.
descriptions.officials_city: City officials are not listed yet. They'll appear here once official records are added.
descriptions.officials_county: County officials are not listed yet. They'll appear here once official records are added.
descriptions.officials_dc: The mayor and council are not listed yet. They'll appear here once official records are added.
descriptions.officials_state: The governor and state lawmakers are not listed yet. They'll appear here once official records are added.
descriptions.officials_territory: The governor and local lawmakers are not listed yet. They'll appear here once official records are added.
descriptions.parish: In Louisiana, parishes are what other states call counties. Parishes often run local courts, property records, the sheriff's office, and some roads.
descriptions.planning_region: Connecticut has no county governments. The Census Bureau uses Connecticut's planning regions in their place. Towns in a region plan some things together, like transportation, but most local services come from each city or town.
descriptions.senate_vacant: One Senate seat for {name} is empty right now. Depending on state law, the governor may appoint someone or voters fill it in a special election.
descriptions.state: {name} is one of the 50 states. Its governor and state legislature make state laws on things like schools, driver's licenses, and state taxes. Everyone in {name} also elects two U.S. Senators, who serve six-year terms in Congress.
descriptions.state_dc: The District of Columbia is the nation's capital. It is not a state, so it has no U.S. Senators, and Congress can review its laws. People here elect a mayor and a council for local matters.
descriptions.state_pr: Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, and people born there are U.S. citizens. It elects its own governor and legislature. It has no U.S. Senators.
